articles.title: 'No Kings' foot soldiers ignore organizers' warning, go all in for Democrats
articles.summary: "No Kings" organizers promote "Vote Blue" and partisan slogans that their own national coalition rulebook explicitly prohibits at Saturday's rallies.
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. – As the high-level organizers of the "No Kings" demonstrations seek to turn their operation into a nationwide get-out-the-vote rally Saturday, their warning to steer clear of partisan messaging that could violate their own rules is falling on deaf ears. A Fox News Digital investigation reveals that, on the ground, the political activation is in fact highly partisan, led by the center-left Indivisible nonprofit that has received millions of dollars of funding from Democratic mega-donor George Soros. "No Kings" organizers didn't respond to a request for comment. The partisan nature of the day's events is important because political experts say the "No Kings" operation reveals a sophisticated electoral strategy: transform the crowds assembled for anti-Trump protests into a durable voter bloc that participates in elections and turns out a "Blue Tsunami" of votes in political battles. But federal election law bars nonprofits, many of which fund the "No Kings" operation, from advocating for particular candidates. Behind today's action, Fox News Digital has identified a sprawling network of 300 progressive advocacy organizations, labor unions, Democratic political operatives and tax-exempt nonprofits with an estimated $2.5 billion in annual revenues, transforming the "No Kings" protest movement into a nationwide voter-mobilization operation of an estimated 3,000 events for Democrats. A review of digital advertisements for Saturday's "No Kings: Vote Early" demonstrations and their organizing rhetoric identifies multiple instances of organizers promoting the very language the coalition's national rulebook forbids in its attempt to create the illusion of nonpartisanship. In Newark, Delaware, Democratic activists from the local Indivisible chapter are encouraging voters to "wear blue" to their 2 p.m. demonstration at the corner of S. College Avenue and W. Main Street, and their "Sign Ideas" include: "Vote Blue Nov. 3," "Vote Early, Vote Blue" and "Time for a Blue Tsunami." NEW MIDTERM BATTLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES Their announcement reads: "💙 Wear blue to signify the blue tsunami we are hoping we will see in Nov!" Some 3,000 miles away, in Roseburg, Ore., Indivisible Douglas County activists are advertising their own "No Kings" rally with suggested signs reading "DOUGLAS COUNTY VOTES BLUE!," "REPUBLICANS HAD THEIR CHANCE!" and "VOTE EARLY. VOTE THEM OUT!" "Be bold. Be direct. Don't hold back," the Oregon organizers tell participants. Those are precisely the kinds of partisan political messages the national "No Kings" coalition has explicitly prohibited. On a Thursday night webinar promoting the protests, a member of Indivisible Colorado Springs told Indivisible co-founders Leah Greenberg and Ezra Levin that the group's event is struggling to attract media attention without focusing on President Donald Trump. Levin replied: "By all means, make it about Trump. Y'all make it about Trump. Create some conflict. Use some strong language. There's nothing about No Kings that says you can't focus on the fascists in the White House." SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES Democratic Party Recruits at 'No Kings' Under "Event Prohibitions," a "Host Toolkit" warns: "Events must not be partisan in nature or make references to preferred election outcomes." It bars "candidate campaign activity," "any political party or political committee attending or helping coordinate the event." The "Event Prohibitions" list bars events from being held at "overtly partisan organizations, or held at campaign offices, political party headquarters, or other locations principally associated with candidate or party political activity." The prohibitions explicitly state: "Events should not be jointly branded with partisan organizations,' and provides as "Examples: Democratic clubs, 'the Lincoln County Democratic Party.'" Yet, in Roseville, Calif., the Placer County Democratic Party in California is explicit in its connection to the "No Kings" voter drive, advertising a canvassing operation specifically tied to Saturday's "No Kings" rally at the Roseville Galleria. The party's website invites activists to attend a morning canvassing session at Harry Crabb Park, saying voters will be gathered at the rally at the Galleria and promising materials to help participants "support our endorsed candidates." On their Democratic Party website, the local party activists describe the "No Kings" rally as "a day of nonpartisan voter participation." ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES The advertisement raises questions about the relationship between the Democratic Party's candidate-support operation and an event whose national organizers expressly prohibit political parties, political committees and candidate campaigns from coordinating activities. In Springfield, Pa., an event listed on the Women's March organizing platform advertises a one-hour "No Kings FOUR" demonstration at 1200 Baltimore Pike. The event calls for voter participation and, in another direct conflict with the national coalition's ban on "vote Blue" appeals, also declares: "Vote Blue. Vote. Make Your Voice Count." FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS Rules They Wrote Themselves The coalition's own documents leave little ambiguity about its official standards. In a five-page "Talking Points + Messaging" guide, organizers instruct participants not to use partisan political language, including telling participants to "vote for Democrats up and down the ballot" or saying, "we can get a Democratic Congress elected in 2026 to resist Trump." It bars any "speaker expressing bias for or against any candidate for office," the guide states. It prohibits candidate campaign activities, including campaign literature, fundraising and coordination with campaign staff. Political parties and political committees are also barred from helping coordinate events. The instructions go beyond conventional warnings against endorsements. Organizers specifically prohibit references to "MAGA politicians" and calls to elect a Democratic Congress. Even urging participants to register as Democrats ahead of the midterms is explicitly forbidden. Another document, "Event Prohibitions + Things to Note," specifically prohibits "vote them out" and "vote Blue" messaging, campaign fundraising and political party coordination. Still, in Kingstowne, Va., Indivisible of Franconia is promoting its Oct. 17 rally at South Van Dorn Street and Kingstowne Village Parkway with the statement: "We vote for leaders to represent our interests—and if they don’t, we need to vote them out." The coalition also prohibits events hosted or co-sponsored by overtly partisan organizations, including Democratic clubs. Its "Election Law FAQs" and "Resources" go further, warning that merely describing an event as "nonpartisan" doesn't establish that it meets the standard. "Saying this doesn’t automatically make it so," the document states. Democratic Infrastructure Behind No Kings The contradictions come as "No Kings" draws on a sprawling coalition of advocacy organizations, labor unions and political activists. In March, Fox News Digital identified about 500 organizations associated with the movement, representing an estimated $3 billion in combined annual revenues. The coalition partner list for today's protests is smaller but continues to include major labor organizations such as the American Federation of Teachers, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, the National Education Association and the Service Employees International Union. It also includes organizations that align with the Democratic Party, including: Indivisible, MoveOn, Planned Parenthood Action Fund, End Citizens United, NextGen America, Our Revolution, Voto Latino and the Democratic Socialists of America. Most of these organizations or their affiliated political committees have histories of substantial spending to support Democratic candidates and causes. Their involvement places organizations with extensive electoral experience inside a coalition now publicly promising to avoid partisan campaign activity. The coalition's breadth also raises questions about how organizers distinguish between participating in a nonpartisan event and advancing the electoral objectives of affiliated political organizations. From a $250,000 Protest to the Ballot Box The political infrastructure was visible during the March 28 flagship No Kings rally in St. Paul, Minn. Fox News Digital documented an estimated $250,000 production operation involving nine vendors, approximately 30 semitrucks, a massive stage, eight video screens and other concert-scale equipment. Roger Fisk, a former Obama and Biden administration political strategist, described himself as a senior adviser to the flagship event and credited its sophisticated media operation with generating hundreds of millions of digital impressions. The event featured Democratic political figures and celebrities, including rock star Bruce Springsteen and actress Jane Fonda, illustrating the extensive organizational and political relationships behind the movement. Former Gov. Tim Walz, Rep. Ilhan Omar and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison – all Democrats – were among the event's political speakers, alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. The involvement of Democratic officials in earlier anti-Trump demonstrations illustrates the movement's close relationship with Democratic political figures. Now the coalition is moving from street demonstrations to voter mobilization. In its October "Host Toolkit," "No Kings" describes Saturday's events as an opportunity to turn protest participation into electoral engagement. "Pivoting our strategy from marching to voting is our movement using the tool available to us when it matters most," the coalition tells organizers. The "Host Toolkit" insists: "Vote Early events are nonpartisan and are designed to increase participation from all eligible voters. The event should not reference, endorse, or oppose any candidate or political party. The event should not coordinate with any campaign or permit campaign materials. The event should comply with all applicable federal, state and local election laws." The campaign calls for voter education, early-voting assistance, volunteer recruitment and election-protection training, with additional organizing sessions scheduled after Oct. 17. The coalition maintains that the effort is intended for all eligible voters, regardless of party preference. Legal Dividing Line The distinction between partisan advocacy and nonpartisan voter education matters particularly for tax-exempt organizations. Under federal law, 501(c)(3) charities are prohibited from supporting or opposing political candidates. Other organizations, including 501(c)(4) advocacy groups and political action committees, operate under different legal restrictions. Indivisible, the coalition's leading organizer, operates through several affiliated entities with different legal structures, including a 501(c)(4) advocacy organization, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and a political action committee. The coalition has scheduled an Oct. 21 training on what happens after the demonstrations, followed by an Oct. 22 session on sustained mobilization and protecting election results. Just two days before the nationwide No Kings demonstrations, Indivisible co-founders Levin and Greenberg discussed the November midterms in openly partisan terms, celebrating Democratic candidates, criticizing Republicans and outlining their hopes for Democratic control of Congress. "Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said, referring to Democratic and Republican candidates, respectively. During the program, Levin, identifying himself as "a Texas Democrat," summarized the organization's immediate priorities: "Right now, we're just full on let's win the election, but after that, we're going to shift." Levin said "you got to let people connect the dots" on the "nonpartisan" messaging. In a webinar last week, Levin was clear about the effort's political and electoral goals to win a "Democratic trifecta" in the White House, the House of Representatives and the Senate, saying: "It ain't over in November. It ain't over in 2027. It ain't over in 2028. We are building towards a national Democratic trifecta in 2029 that ushers in an age of accountability and reform..." articles.title: Income inequality at Obama Foundation, as brass thrives and rank and file seeks union
articles.summary: Half of the Obama Foundation's reported workforce topped $100,000 in pay, outpacing five other presidential nonprofits examined in recent tax filings.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The beleaguered Obama Foundation has an income inequality problem: While half of its employees earn six-figure salaries, led by CEO Valerie Jarrett at $771,000, dozens at the other end of the scale are fighting for union representation. The workplace disparity comes to light just as Fox News Digital reported that the long-delayed Obama Presidential Center's price tag hit $1 billion — nearly triple the original estimate for the Chicago facility. The Obama Foundation, former President Barack Obama's private nonprofit, reported 172 employees receiving more than $100,000 in salary in its 2025 tax filing — roughly half its 342 reported employees. Jarrett, one of former President Barack Obama's closest advisors and a former senior White House official, has led the Obama Foundation since 2021, overseeing the final years of construction of the Presidential Center on Chicago's South Side. OBAMA'S BILLION-DOLLAR BABY: CHICAGO CENTER'S PRICE TAG HITS MONUMENTAL MILESTONE, TRIPLING ORIGINAL ESTIMATE Her total pay rose by around $15,500 from 2024 and she is one of at least four of the nonprofit's 10 highest-paid executives with previous ties to the Obama White House or campaign. "The Foundation pays our employees rates that are competitive with the market," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "We have more than 500 employees worldwide, roughly 300 of whom are based at the Center." The current workforce of more than 500 is substantially larger than the 342 employees reported in the Obama Foundation's 2025 tax filing, which covers the year ending nearly six months before the Presidential Center opened in June. The nonprofit did not provide an updated payroll breakdown. The Obama Foundation saw its annual payroll and benefits bill come in at $50.4 million in 2025, soaring from $18.5 million in 2018. The nonprofit brought in approximately $159 million in revenue last year, of which nearly $151 million consisted of contributions and grants. The spending surge came as the Obama Foundation expanded its leadership and civic programs at home and abroad while racing to finish the beleaguered Presidential Center. The sprawling 19.3-acre campus sits on publicly owned parkland in Chicago's Jackson Park. WATCH: Professor breaks down Obama Foundation's finances amid $1B Presidential Center costs Expert view Brian Mittendorf, an accounting professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit finances, said the proportion of Obama Foundation employees earning more than $100,000 stood out compared with a typical nonprofit, but noted that the organization relies heavily on specialized staff. "That's clearly higher percentage than your average nonprofit," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "But here we're dealing with a nonprofit that's probably very expertise heavy. It's very heavy on like the think tank side. And as you look at a think tank, it would look very differently than say a local food bank." Mittendorf said the Obama Foundation's employees likely possess specialized skills that could command substantial pay elsewhere. "So it does reflect that a lot of their employees are ones that they would consider having an outside opportunity that would justify them getting paid at that level," he said. "Like I said, it is atypical for a standard nonprofit, but probably not that unusual for a nonprofit of its type." The Obama Foundation also reported a higher proportion of employees receiving more than $100,000 than five other presidential nonprofits examined by Fox News Digital. Roughly half its reported workforce exceeded that threshold in 2025, compared with 37% at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, 29% at the Carter Center, 23% at the Clinton Foundation, 13% at the Reagan Foundation and 10% at the George & Barbara Bush Foundation, according to their respective 2024 tax filings, the most recent available for the review. OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER'S $470M SAFETY NET UNDER SCRUTINY AS SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY'RE OWED MILLIONS Executive pay Jarrett's salary rose from approximately $581,000 when she took over as CEO in 2021 to $740,000 in 2022, remaining at that level through 2024 before climbing to nearly $755,000 in 2025. For comparison, Fox News Digital reviewed the latest available tax filings from five other major presidential foundations, all of which reported lower CEO salaries than Jarrett's $771,000 in 2025. The Reagan Foundation paid its CEO approximately $735,000 and the Carter Center $531,000 for fiscal years ending in 2025, while the George W. Bush Presidential Center paid its top officer $661,000, the George & Barbara Bush Foundation $426,600 and the Clinton Foundation $425,000 for 2024. Beyond Jarrett, several former Obama administration officials continued to collect hefty six-figure paychecks at the Obama Foundation. Christina Tchen, former chief of staff to first lady Michelle Obama, received approximately $431,000 in salary in 2025, while Michael Strautmanis, a former Obama campaign and White House aide, collected approximately $404,000. Laura Lucas Magnuson, a former White House communications official, received approximately $396,000. Other top earners included Robbin Cohen, who received approximately $666,000. Cohen previously led Pritzker Realty Group, founded by billionaire Democratic donor and former Obama commerce secretary Penny Pritzker, a cousin of Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Former Cook County chief financial officer Ammar Rizki received approximately $400,000. The Obama Foundation defended its executive salary practices. "The Board of Directors uses comparability data and a compensation consultant to review and approve the compensation of the CEO, officers and key employees on an annual basis," Bittner told Fox News Digital. OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25 The nonprofit also pointed to higher pay for top executives at other major charitable institutions, including approximately $2 million for the Getty Trust's president and CEO, $1.7 million for the Rockefeller Foundation's president and $1.5 million for the Mellon Foundation's president, citing figures from their recent tax filings. The Getty Trust, however, operates on a vastly different financial scale, with a multibillion-dollar endowment compared with the Obama Foundation's approximately $14.2 million in reported endowment funds at the end of 2025. Asked whether Jarrett's pay was excessive, Mittendorf said the answer was subjective, particularly given the Obama Foundation's size and financial resources. "This is not an unusual amount that to see for a highest paid employee for a director or a CEO," he said, noting the nonprofit's net assets exceeded $1 billion. Mittendorf acknowledged, however, that substantial executive pay at charitable organizations can attract criticism. "So I think you see criticism from time to time of executive directors that get paid at this level, not that they could not get paid similar amounts in the private sector, but that there is a belief that in the nonprofit sector, the pay should not just reflect what you would get in the public sector, but something more modest," he said. "It's quite common, though, for an organization of this size." Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan, a longtime critic of the Obama Foundation's use of public parkland for the private organization, accused the nonprofit of enriching Obama's inner circle at taxpayers' expense. "The Obama Center is another far-left political operation that acts as a non-profit while using taxpayer dollars to make Barack Obama's inner circle rich," Grogan told Fox News Digital. The Obama Foundation maintains that construction of the Presidential Center was privately funded and that its operating costs are covered by revenues and private donations. Public funds have also supported infrastructure improvements surrounding the campus. Workers push to unionize The hefty executive paychecks come as rank-and-file Obama Foundation employees push to unionize, alleging rolled-back benefits and mounting workloads. Workers also claim deteriorating conditions have driven experienced colleagues to leave, taking valuable institutional knowledge with them and piling more work onto those who remain. The employees, organized under Obama Workers United with AFSCME Council 31, include visitor services and cleaning staff, museum and technology workers, and employees involved in the nonprofit's educational and global programs. "Amidst increasing workloads we have seen our benefits rolled back and support from leadership to be minimal," the workers wrote in a public letter. SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY’RE OWED MILLIONS, FACE FINANCIAL RUIN, AFTER HELPING BUILD OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The workers also urged Obama Foundation leadership to respect their right to organize and refrain from spending money on anti-union lawyers, messaging or meetings. The Obama Foundation said it supports employees' right to organize. "We are deeply committed to the fundamental right of workers to organize and make their voices heard," the nonprofit said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "As members of our staff explore union representation, we approach this process with immense gratitude for their contributions, deep respect for unions, and a sincere commitment to working collaboratively with our partners in labor."

articles.title: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
articles.summary: Federal agents raided Ilhan Omar's D.C. home, seizing her phone, computers and passport as part of a criminal probe into immigration fraud.
articles.body: It was a week of legal turmoil for one of America's most recognizable members of Congress. Early Monday morning, federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. The raid was part of an ongoing criminal probe into Omar's immigration status, with sources telling Fox News Digital that authorities are scrutinizing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out paperwork for her to become a U.S. citizen. A day later, U.S. Attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., Jeannine Pirro, announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION Fox News Digital breaks down what we know so far about each investigation: Financial Disclosure Investigation: In May 2025, Omar filed financial disclosure forms for the year 2024, a required for every member of Congress to complete every year. I showed that she had between $6 million and $30 million in assets connected to two businesses run by her husband, Tim Mynett. One was was a venture capital firm, and the other a California winery. Her financial disclosures from the year prior, covering 2023, said those assets were only valued at between $15,000 and $51,000 total. The now-defunct winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year. The massive reported spike in net worth over the one-year span raised eyebrows, leading a watchdog group called the National Legal and Policy Center to file a complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct in February of this year. 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP Less than a month after the complaint was filed, Omar amended her 2025 disclosure form. The new filing reduced the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000, and said the businesses had zero value after accounting for liabilities. ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT Omar blamed an accounting error, and has since repeatedly insisted that she is not a millionaire. In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures. But the hubbub caught the eye of Pirro, who confirmed on Fox News' "America Reports" Tuesday that her office is investigating the discrepancies. Further details about the investigation have not yet been released. Criminal Immigration Probe: Monday's judicially authorized raid of Omar's Washington, D.C. home sent shockwaves through the political world, with many critics calling it politically motivated because it occurred three weeks before November's general elections. The Trump administration has denied those accusations. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ HSI agents spent several hours at Omar's home, and the Wall Street Journal reported that the lawmaker's personal cell phone, computers and passport were seized during the search. She has not been seen publicly since before the raid. Sources told Fox News Digital that investigators are scrutinizing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork when Omar was become a U.S. citizen decades ago. The Journal also reported that the goal of the probe is to strip Omar of her citizenship. A dozen people, including family members, were subpoenaed in relation to the investigation. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE "Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully," President Donald Trump said Monday of the raid. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me." "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is ... a non-country, and then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution," he continued. "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it." On Tuesday in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital after rallying for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, Vice President JD Vance echoed a similar sentiment. "We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," Vance said. "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this. And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to." ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION Vance made it clear taking that unprecedented step of denaturalizing a sitting member of Congress is possible, but only if the law requires it based on the facts of the case. "And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," Vance said. "We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime." "But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law." A spokesperson for Omar did not return multiple requests for comment throughout the week. However, Omar has responded on social media. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said. articles.title: Pedro Sánchez se 'declara' a Begoña Gómez con un beso en pleno mitin: “Que lo escuchen alto y claro: te quiero”
articles.standfirst: El presidente dedicó parte de su discurso a su esposa en plena campaña por el 29N
articles.summary: El presidente dedicó parte de su discurso a su esposa en plena campaña por el 29N
articles.body: Los mítines suelen estar hechos de promesas, ataques al rival y llamadas al voto. Pero de vez en cuando, en medio del discurso político, se cuela un momento que nada tiene que ver con el programa electoral y que acaba robando todo el protagonismo. Eso ha ocurrido este sábado en Fuenlabrada (Madrid). Pedro Sánchez, recién proclamado candidato del PSOE a las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, dedicó una parte de su intervención a su esposa, Begoña Gómez, que le acompañaba en el acto de precampaña. El presidente del Gobierno se dirigió a ella ante la militancia para agradecerle su apoyo. “Quería darte las gracias por ser mi esposa, la madre de mis hijas y por ser mi mujer”, afirmó. Y lo remató con una frase pensada para que se oyera fuera del pabellón: “Que lo escuchen alto y claro: te quiero”. Sánchez selló sus palabras con un beso a Gómez, que el público celebró entre aplausos y gritos de “¡Qué bonito!”. Ella, por su parte, animó a los asistentes con los brazos en alto antes de fundirse en un abrazo con su marido y terminar por un beso muy ovacionado por los asistentes. El líder socialista también aludió a los procesos judiciales que afectan a su entorno. Según dijo, los intentos de quebrarlos solo han conseguido que estén “más unidos que nunca”. La declaración llega mientras Gómez está pendiente de juicio por presuntos delitos de tráfico de influencias y malversación. Algunos medios lo interpretaron también como una respuesta a sus críticos. El gesto coincidió con una jornada en la que los socialistas quisieron exhibir cohesión. El Comité Federal del partido proclamó por unanimidad a Sánchez como candidato a la Presidencia del Gobierno y ratificó las listas al Congreso y al Senado. Además, el PSOE y Frente Amplio sellaron un acuerdo para concurrir juntos al Senado bajo el nombre de Senado de Progreso, con el objetivo de disputar al Partido Popular la mayoría que mantiene en la Cámara Alta.

articles.title: Your bumper sticker could help Flock cameras track where you go — new bill aims to stop it
articles.summary: Rep. Pat Harrigan's bill would require warrants for ALPR searches, delete records within 24 hours and ban tracking political or religious stickers.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Americans are sounding the alarm over privacy concerns surrounding Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that can snap photos of cars and track locations, and one GOP lawmaker is moving to close the gaps. Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., introduced a bill Thursday that would ban ALPR searches targeting political or religious messages on vehicles, require warrants for most searches, mandate that records be deleted within 24 hours and prohibit vendors from selling or sharing location data. "When you consider that these systems track everything that you do, where you work, where your kids go to school, where you even go to church, I think it's pretty easy to understand why people are concerned," Harrigan told Fox News Digital. "So that's an extraordinary amount of information about somebody that the government has that has never committed a crime." POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN' Flock cameras and other ALPRs have drawn widespread debate. Law enforcement uses them in criminal investigations to collect searchable license plate, location and other vehicle data that allow officers to search by location and identify vehicles matching a suspect’s vehicle description. Critics believe they raise constitutional concerns by tracking drivers without consent, while supporters say they are needed for crime prevention. President Donald Trump has voiced support for Flock cameras, telling reporters on Sept. 13 that he "sort of" likes them because of their use by law enforcement despite some people calling them "an infringement." Harrigan's bill would impose restrictions on all ALPR systems, including prohibiting government agencies from categorizing vehicles by "expressive attributes" like political or religious bumper stickers, flags or decals. HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK’S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS "At the end of the day, they have nothing to do with whether you committed a crime or not," Harrigan said. "As all of this data comes in and is vacuumed in by the government, it becomes searchable, particularly with the new technologies that we have surrounding artificial intelligence." That means messages ranging from "Back the Blue" to "Jesus Saves" or "Black Lives Matter" could not be turned into searchable data. The bill would also block ALPR searches targeting political or religious activity, civil immigration violations, parking or non-moving traffic violations, debts and other civil penalties. As ALPR technology expands, Flock Safety says its systems can detect bumper stickers but cannot identify their type, "like a political party or a house of worship." However, its AI-powered FreeForm search allows users to search vehicle characteristics "in plain terms," raising questions about how bumper stickers and other markings could be used to identify vehicles. The company said safeguards are designed to block searches for vehicles based on political or religious bumper stickers and symbols. The bill would require law enforcement to have a probable cause warrant in most searches, with exceptions for immediate threats to someone’s life or safety. Records would have to be deleted within 24 hours, with exceptions for warrants, emergencies and court orders. It would also require agencies to log ALPR searches, publish annual reports and undergo audits. States without qualifying protections could lose 10% of certain federal criminal justice funding. Additionally, vendors would be prohibited from selling ALPR data or using it to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. And for Americans worried about their Fourth Amendment rights, the bill would offer legal protections, allowing people to sue over illegal searches for at least $1,000 per violation and keep illegally obtained evidence out of court. TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT MOVES TO CUT STATE FUNDING FOR AI-POWERED FLOCK CAMERAS AMID PRIVACY CONCERNS In August, The Washington Post found that at least 50 officers had been accused or charged with misusing license plate readers. Some reportedly used them to spy on romantic partners, exes or other women, with Flock’s system used in 46 cases. Harrigan said the bill would not stop the technology from being used as an investigative tool and would instead place limits on how far law enforcement can go. "Simultaneously, when we have technology that can benefit humanity and our experience here as Americans and make America safer, we should leverage that. But we have to strike the right balance," he said. He said he believes lawmakers can get behind the bill "regardless of your political philosophy." "Protecting Americans from criminals and protecting their constitutional rights, to me, those are two core responsibilities of government," he said. "And I think that that's something that members on both sides of the aisle can get behind."
